statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: This chapter asks what a neural network *does* to the numbers that live in space, and draws each operation as a picture.
statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: The claim: **nearly every layer in a modern network is a single geometric move**.
statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: Once you can see the move, you can predict what the layer is for, where it can fail, and what it costs.
statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: * **The inner product** — a dot product is a *measurement of alignment*; its shadow, the Gram matrix, is where “similarity” is stored \cite{scholkopf2002learning}.
statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: * **Projection** — fitting anything is the same move: the best fit is the *shadow* the data throws onto a subspace, and the error is the piece left standing.
statements.section: One picture for the whole chapter

statements.quote: * **The singular value decomposition** — every matrix is a rotation, a set of pure stretches, and a rotation again; the stretches *are* the shape of the map \cite{svd_wiki}.

statements.quote: Read the factorisation as a story about a circle:

statements.quote: Two facts turn the picture into engineering:
statements.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

statements.quote: * **Rank is the number of non-zero singular values.** If $\sigma_2 = 0$ the ellipse collapses to a line and the map forgets an input dimension — its image is lower-dimensional.

statements.quote: Keeping only the top $r$ terms, $A \approx \sum_{i\le r}\sigma_i\, u_i v_i^{\top}$, is the *best* rank-$r$ approximation: it keeps the biggest stretches and drops the smallest \cite{svd_wiki}.
statements.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

statements.quote: * **Singular values are the “true sizes.”** Unlike eigenvalues, they are always real and non-negative and are defined for *any* rectangular matrix.
statements.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

statements.quote: The ratio $\kappa = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$, the **condition number**, measures how much more one direction is stretched than another — it controls how ill-conditioned the map is, and how sensitive its output is to noise.
statements.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

statements.quote: That truncation is optimal in a precise sense: among all matrices of rank at most $r$, the truncated SVD is closest in both the spectral and Frobenius norms.

statements.quote: Training a model is walking downhill on a loss landscape $L$.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: At any point $w$ the **gradient** $\nabla L(w) = (\partial L/\partial w_1, \dots, \partial L/\partial w_d)$ is a vector pointing the way the function climbs *fastest*, so $-\nabla L$ points straight *downhill*.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Is the gradient actually the steepest way, or just a convenient choice?
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: The answer is geometric — it is the inner-product identity pointed at a function.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: The **directional derivative** of $L$ in a unit direction $d$ is an inner product (\cite[Boyd & Vandenberghe, Applied Linear Algebra, Ch.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: 36]{boyd2018appliedlinearalgebra}), using two geometric signs: $a \parallel b$ (*parallel to*) and $a \perp b$ (*perpendicular to*):
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: So $\langle \nabla L, d\rangle$ is largest when $d$ points *along* $\nabla L$ and most negative when $d$ points *against* it.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Steepest ascent is $+\nabla L$ and steepest descent is $-\nabla L$ — not by choice, but because the inner product *forces* the steepest direction to be the gradient.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Cauchy wrote this down in 1847 as the method of steepest descent, a century before neural networks \cite{cauchy1847}.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Strictly, Cauchy's 1847 note treats simultaneous equations by minimising a sum of squares; it is not a general nonlinear-descent method.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: The name "steepest descent" and the convergence theory came later, with Hadamard's 1907–08 method (\cite[Hadamard, 1908]{hadamard1908}) and the mid-20th-century optimisation literature.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: The constrained version — project the gradient back onto the feasible set — is Rosen's gradient-projection method (1960) (\cite[Rosen, 1960]{rosen1960}), the direct ancestor of the projection step in modern constrained optimisers.

statements.quote: In 1847 he proposed moving a point *against the gradient* to solve systems of equations and to fit by least squares \cite{cauchy1847} — the move later christened the **method of steepest descent**, and the same move every gradient-based optimizer makes on a loss landscape.}
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Read the same identity differently: the gradient is **perpendicular to the level sets** of $L$ — the “same loss” contours.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: Moving along a contour keeps $L$ constant, so its direction $d$ satisfies $\langle \nabla L, d\rangle = 0$, i.e. $d \perp \nabla L$.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: This is why a *curved* landscape is hard to descend: in a narrow valley the gradient points *across* the valley rather than down it, so a plain step zig-zags.
statements.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

statements.quote: A neural network is a stack of functions $f$.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: A function has a **symmetry** when some operation on its input changes the input but the output moves in a predictable, *structured* way.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Write a symmetry as $\sigma$ and its action on an input $x$ as $\sigma \cdot x$ (here the dot means “apply $\sigma$ to $x$,” not multiplication).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * **Invariant** — the output does not change: $f(\sigma \cdot x) = f(x)$ for a symmetry $\sigma$ (say, reordering the inputs).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The output “forgets” the symmetry.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * **Equivariant** — the output changes *the same way* the input did: $f(\sigma \cdot x) = \sigma \cdot f(x)$.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The function “commutes” with the symmetry.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Write the equivariance condition as a diagram that **commutes**: do the symmetry first, then the function, or the function first, then the symmetry — both paths land on the same point.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The commuting square is the whole idea of equivariance, and it is *geometric*: $f$ and the symmetry $\sigma$ are two motions of space that get along.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The modern definition is Klein's.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: In the *Erlangen Programme* of 1872 he proposed that a geometry *is* the study of what a group of transformations leaves invariant (\cite[Klein, 1872]{klein1872erlangen}).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Read backwards, that is the neural-network question: choose the group — translations, permutations, rotations — and the architecture is the family of functions that respect it.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Noether's 1918 theorem is the physicist's cousin: every continuous symmetry of an action yields a conserved quantity (\cite[Noether, 1918]{noether1918}).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Weyl's *Classical Groups* (1939) catalogued the invariants themselves (\cite[Weyl, 1939]{weyl1939classicalgroups}).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: These are not exotic — they are *forced*.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: **Deep Sets** \cite{zaheer2017deepsets} proved that any function of a *set* of inputs that is permutation-invariant must factor as “map each item, add them up, then pool”:
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: and it gives the matching condition for equivariance.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: “Map, sum, pool” is not a design choice — it is *the* shape any invariant or equivariant function on a set must have.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The theorem's hypothesis matters: for a countable universe the sum decomposition is exact; for uncountable domains the paper proves it only for sets of fixed size and conjectures the general case (\cite[Zaheer et al., 2017]{zaheer2017deepsets}).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The equivariant form is different: for a linear layer it forces weight sharing, $\Theta=\lambda I+\gamma\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}$.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: This matters because **weight sharing is equivariance in disguise**, and attention is *permutation-equivariant* rather than symmetric:
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * A **CNN** shares one kernel across every location — translation-equivariance: shift the input and the feature map shifts the same way (see [Computer Vision](computer_vision)).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: The convolution section’s “sliding dot product” is the *mechanism*; this section is the *reason it is allowed*.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * **Pooling** (mean, max) is the invariant readout: reorder what you pool over and the number does not move.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * **Attention** is permutation-equivariant over the token set: shuffle the tokens and every output token and attention weight shuffles along.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: Order is not something attention knows, which is why position must be *added in explicitly* (see [Positional Embeddings](positionalembeddingslab)).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: * The same logic reaches **graphs**: a GNN is equivariant under re-labeling the vertices, which is why its basic form is message-passing — a sum over neighbors (the broader program is **geometric deep learning** \cite{bronstein2021geometric}).
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

statements.quote: A caution on the word "symmetric": attention is permutation-equivariant, not symmetric.
statements.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention
